title: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
content:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.
Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.
First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.
Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board.
Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.
Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them an 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.
Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.
Here’s what all that looks like:
The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.
At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.
The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.
If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.

report.summary: Anthropic's pre-IPO governance hands a mission trust, its seven founders and the board layered control, leaving public shareholders with little say.
report.background: Anthropic was founded in 2021 as a public benefit corporation with a mission of AI safety, and it is now approaching an IPO. Dual-class and founder-controlled share structures are standard in Silicon Valley — Musk's Tesla and Zuckerberg's Meta are familiar examples — but Anthropic has stacked several mechanisms on top of one another: a public benefit charter, a Long Term Benefit Trust that elects a majority of the board, a founder block holding 50.1% of voting power, and a board committee that can send trust nominations to an employee vote. The design echoes OpenAI's 2023 board crisis, when Sam Altman was briefly fired and then reinstated after staff rallied behind him. Anthropic appears to have formalized that employee-power dynamic into its charter, raising the question of what, precisely, a public investor is buying.
key_points: Public benefit corporation status shields the board from shareholder suits when it weighs AI safety against profit. Directors can justify decisions that reduce returns if they serve the stated mission, narrowing the grounds on which ordinary investors could challenge them.

The Long Term Benefit Trust, chaired by Neil Shah and including Ben Bernanke and Richard Fontaine, holds a share class that elects and removes a majority of the board, the Class T directors. It is self-perpetuating: sitting members fill their own vacancies.

Anthropic's seven founders jointly hold special stock giving a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power and the right to elect three directors. If the founders split, their votes revert to common-stock proportions, which could unexpectedly amplify ordinary shareholders.

The board can push back on the trust. If the LTBT names or removes a 'Specified' director without cause, the nominating committee may reject the move and hand the decision to employees — a formal version of the staff revolt that saved Sam Altman at OpenAI.

Both control layers sunset. Founders can release control ten years after the IPO, or it ends automatically when fewer than three remain. The trust persists until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it or it steps down with board approval.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic is setting a template: frontier labs are increasingly structured as mission-locked entities that raise public capital without ceding public control. Expect copycat charters and louder investor debate over whether such governance deserves a valuation discount. For developers, near-term product and API decisions are unlikely to change, but long-term safety policy — model release pacing, usage restrictions, compute commitments — is insulated from market pressure, which matters for anyone building on Claude. For regular users, the structure says who can course-correct if a model is deployed recklessly: ultimately a small trust and a founders' bloc, not shareholders or regulators. The employee override is the most novel and least predictable element, since it depends on internal culture rather than capital.
report.tools: To follow this, read Anthropic's S-1 and charter filings via SEC EDGAR full-text search, and track Class T and founder share classes in later proxy statements. Governance researchers can use OpenCorporates for entity structure and proxy-advisor reports from ISS and Glass Lewis. On the technical side, Anthropic's published Responsible Scaling Policy and its open-source releases are the practical way to see whether mission language translates into shipping behavior.
